title: AGL hit by class action; Austal jumps on takeover talks
full_text:
That’s all from The Australian’s rolling coverage of business and markets news for Wednesday, October 14.
An $8.4m August share sale by CBA chief Matt Comyn to settle personal affairs has one major investor asking if the ‘inevitable transition’ will keep the banking leader strong enough to justify the high premiums paid by shareholders.
After eight years in the top job, Mr Comyn is a central presence at the bank and has a high-profile role in its engagement with government and other stakeholders, the Australian Shareholder Association said ahead of the annual general meeting in Sydney on Wednesday.
CBA CEO Matt Comyn. Picture: Adam Yip.
At the 2025 AGM, the bank appeared to have locked in Mr Comyn’s earliest departure at least until 2029. At that meeting, chairman Paul O’Malley was re-elected for a final three-year term, finishing in October 2028, and had indicated the selection of a new CEO would be left to the next chair.
David Murray was CBA’s longest serving chief executive at 13 years.
But Mr Comyn’s share sale in August this year, on the back of a split from wife, led the ASA to ask CBA management a key question: “when the inevitable transition of the CEO occurs, will the CBA franchise remain strong enough for investors to continue to pay its high P/E (price/earnings?”
Most analysts see CBA’s key issue is its valuation, trading on elevated multiples (~26x P/E) and a strong premium (~50-70 per cent) to peers.
In pre-AGM discussions in late September, Mr O’Malley told the ASA it has “succession scenarios in place should he depart earlier than anticipated and has developed a pool of potential internal successors”.
While the Australian mortgage market and strong market position remains central to CBA’s earnings, the question for the ASA is “how much of its current profitability is genuinely sustainable”.
CBA reported a 7 per cent year-on-year increase in FY26 cash profit to a record $11bn, meeting S&P’s expectations.
That result has come as Mr Comyn’s total remuneration increased to $9.14m, including $5.06m in deferred awards, up from $7.02m. Shareholders will approve another 24,384 in restricted share units and performance rights for FY27 for Mr Comyn, subject to tests.
Signs of softer lending demand, pressure on household spending and competition for loans and deposits will test its ability to protect margins without weakening credit standards, the ASA noted. And Macquarie’s growth as a significant player is a threat too.
On governance and culture, the ASA raised the question of accounting giant PwC being its lead audit partner since 2008. A change is expected in 12 months, within the regulated 5-year time period.
But CBA has said it is “limited in its choice of auditor” because only three Australian-based professional services firms have the capabilities to audit large financial institutions, together with the international presence to provide global analysis of financial firms, particularly those operating in the US.
CBA’s belief is that PwC currently fulfils these requirements better than any other firm.
The AGM proceedings are expected to run smoothly after CBA gave into the Finance Sector Union’s push for “a genuine pay rise” on Tuesday. The union claimed the bank’s offer was made to avoid the prospect of CBA workers protesting at the event.
CBA presented the union with an improved offer that will see workers on the lowest pay band get a 13 per cent pay increase over three years – the highest pay outcome in the banking sector.
The new offer also includes up to an additional 6.5 per cent guaranteed pay rise for higher paid Tier 3 and 4 employees compared to what CBA was previously offering. The FSU said it was “an offer befitting Australia’s richest bank”. The offer still requires a formal vote of all CBA workers.
Shares in CBA last at $154.50.
